reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Most thoracic aortic aneurysms are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally on chest imaging performed for other reasons
Symptoms, when present, reflect local compression and may include chest or back pain, hoarseness, dysphagia, or stridor
Ascending and arch aneurysms are often linked to degeneration of the aortic media, while descending aneurysms are more commonly atherosclerotic
Connective tissue disorders such as Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes, bicuspid aortic valve, and a family history predispose to earlier and more aggressive disease
CT angiography and MR angiography define aneurysm extent, diameter, and involvement of aortic branches for surveillance and operative planning
Repair thresholds are based on maximal diameter, growth rate, symptoms, and underlying aetiology, with lower thresholds for connective tissue disease
Blood pressure control and cardiovascular risk-factor management slow expansion and reduce dissection risk during surveillance
Open surgical and endovascular (thoracic endovascular aortic repair) approaches are selected according to aneurysm location, anatomy, and patient fitness
reference.pathophysiology: Thoracic aortic aneurysm is a permanent localised dilatation of the thoracic aorta resulting from weakening of the aortic wall. Degeneration of medial elastin and smooth muscle, driven by genetic connective tissue disorders, bicuspid valve-associated aortopathy, atherosclerosis, or ageing, reduces wall integrity. According to the law of Laplace, increasing diameter raises wall tension, promoting further expansion in a self-perpetuating cycle. As the wall weakens it becomes vulnerable to acute dissection, in which an intimal tear allows blood to track within the media, and ultimately to rupture.
additionalDifferentials: Aortic intramural haematoma or penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer
Acute coronary syndrome (for chest pain presentations)
additionalInvestigations: CT angiography of the thoracic aorta for diameter, extent, and branch involvement
MR angiography as a radiation-sparing alternative for surveillance
Transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiography for the aortic root and valve
Genetic evaluation and family screening when a heritable aortopathy is suspected
Assessment of cardiac and respiratory fitness prior to intervention
redFlags: Sudden severe chest or back pain suggesting acute dissection or impending or actual rupture, a surgical emergency
Haemodynamic instability or syncope indicating rupture or tamponade
New hoarseness, stridor, or dysphagia from rapid enlargement
Rapid interval growth or diameter exceeding operative thresholds
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on aneurysm size, growth rate, and aetiology; small aneurysms often remain stable under surveillance, whereas large or rapidly expanding lesions carry a high risk of dissection or rupture. Elective repair markedly improves survival compared with the very high mortality of rupture, though operative risk varies with aneurysm extent and comorbidity.
pitfalls: Dismissing incidental thoracic aortic dilatation without arranging appropriate surveillance
Applying general size thresholds to patients with connective tissue disease who warrant earlier repair
Attributing acute chest and back pain solely to cardiac causes and missing dissection
Neglecting family screening in heritable aortopathies
